newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Farmers threaten Milosevic with road blockade.
newsitem.headline: Farmers threaten Milosevic with road blockade.

text.p: Farmers blocked a main road in northern Serbia on Monday and warned President Slobodan Milosevic, already embattled by an election rigging crisis, they would paralyse the country.

Djordje Garabandic, president of the Independent Farmers Union, said the protest was to force the government to pay money it owes to the farmers and was unconnected with five weeks of opposition street protests against Milosevic.

As 20 tractors blocked the road between Novi Sad and Zrenjanin, Garabandic told Reuters: "Today's blockade is a blockade of warning. Tomorrow we are planning to blackade all the roads and all the factories."

Wider action by the farmers could threaten Milosevic's plans to bring thousands of government supporters by bus to Belgrade on Tuesday for a rally the ruling socialists intend should show they have broad popular backing.

Students and the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition have been waging a campaign of street protests since accusing the socialists of cheating them of victories in Belgrade and other towns in municipal elections on November 17.
Workers have mostly ignored the intelligentsia-based marches in Belgrade but the farmers' threat to intensify the confrontation boded ill for Milosevic's efforts to regain the political initiative.

Although the opposition demonstrations have been peaceful and Milosevic has not unleashed his police, the socialists' plan to hold their rally in central Belgrade within 100 yards of the opposition demonstration threatened an explosive mix.
Student protest leader Mira Milosevic said: "We are expecting half a million people on either side. You can imagine what could happen. It is very dangerous just to throw your people on the street."
Support for the opposition demonstrations peaked at around 200,000 people but has fallen to about half.
Zajedno said the proximity of the two demonstrations with police keeping them apart increased the danger of provocations which could give security forces an opportunity to intervene.

Zajedno said socialist sources told it that up to 400,000 people from all over Serbia would join the pro-Milosevic demonstration to show the "power and force" of the party which has ruled without a break for half a century.
There was no official comment on reports that Milosevic, who rarely appears in public but always speaks decisively when he does, would address the rally.

A mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) spent the weekend in Belgrade investigating what member called "pretty impressive evidence" of socialist election rigging.
It is expected to issue a verdict within a week on Zajedno's demand, supported by the United States and other Western governmments, for the election results to be honoured.

Opposition sources who met the OSCE team said their expectation was that Milosevic would surrender the claimed towns, including Belgrade, but would call new elections early next year to try to recover them.
